transcript.content: Hello, welcome. What brings you in to see me today?

I came in because I can’t stop focusing on how uneven and puffy the left side of my face looks, especially on video calls and in salsa photos. Everyone tells me they don’t see it, but I do, and it’s starting to affect my work and social life.
Do you find yourself frequently checking your face in mirrors, cameras, or other reflective surfaces throughout the day?

Yes. Before meetings or going out, I keep opening the camera preview and changing the angle or lighting to see if that side looks better. I’ll fix my hair around it, retake pictures, and ask friends if I look strange. Sometimes I do it so much that I’m late, or I feel too drained to go at all.
Deep down, do you ever consider that the unevenness might not be as bad as you see it, or are you completely certain that it really is that noticeable?

I mean, everyone tells me they don’t notice it, so part of me knows they might be right. But when I see myself on video or in photos, the left side looks really uneven and puffy to me. It feels noticeable enough that I can’t just ignore it.
Besides your concerns about your face, do you experience repetitive, unwanted thoughts or feel compelled to repeat routines like checking locks or washing hands?
Not that I’ve noticed. My checking is really just about my face and how it looks.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with persistent preoccupation with a perceived defect in appearance (perceived asymmetry and puffiness of the left side of the face) that is not observable or appears slight to others. This preoccupation is accompanied by repetitive behaviors (frequent checking on camera previews, adjusting angles/lighting, camouflaging with hair, reassurance seeking) causing significant distress and impairment in social and occupational functioning, consistent with body dysmorphic disorder classified under hypochondriacal disorder (F45.2) in ICD-10.

confirmed_symptoms: Preoccupation with perceived unevenness and puffiness on the left side of the face that others do not notice
Frequent checking of appearance using camera preview
Adjusting lighting and camera angles repeatedly
Camouflaging with hair to hide perceived flaw

additional_requirements: Absence of general obsessive-compulsive checking or contamination rituals (rules out typical OCD)
Insight preserved (acknowledges that others may be right and defect might not be as severe)
